steps.body: Remember the strange landing? 2/4 stood on the very same spot as 1/2. Two fractions are **equivalent** when they name the SAME point — the same amount. Not roughly equal, not close: one spot on the line, wearing two names.
Build your own equal fraction. Drag the two sliders until your bar's shaded length matches the target half.

widget.prompt: Slide numerator and denominator to make a fraction equal to 1/2.
widget.successFeedback: Equal! The numbers are bigger but the shaded length is exactly the same as 1/2 — an equivalent fraction.
widget.lowFeedback: Your shaded bar is shorter than the target half. Shade more — raise the numerator, or use fewer parts.
widget.highFeedback: Your shaded bar is longer than half. Shade less — lower the numerator, or split into more parts.

predict.prompt: The bar starts at 1/1. Before you touch it: is 1/1 more or less of the bar than 1/2?
predict.reveal: With the same whole, the bar settles it: 1/1 covers more than 1/2. Count of pieces and size of pieces work together — neither alone decides the amount.

cml.actionGoal: Repartition the same whole and connect the bar, number-line point, and fraction symbol.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: Double both the shaded parts and total parts. What changes visually, and what stays at the same number-line point?

explanation.prompt: Why can two different-looking fractions be equivalent?

options.label: They name the same portion of the same whole and land at the same magnitude.
options.feedback: Exactly. Partition count may change while magnitude stays fixed.

options.label: A fraction with a larger denominator is always larger.
options.feedback: That describes a surface feature, not the mathematical relationship that must remain true. Partition count may change while magnitude stays fixed.

steps.body: Find 1/2's other name on a sixths line.

widget.prompt: This 0→1 trip is cut into SIXTHS. Slide to the spot where 1/2 lives — count your sixth-jumps.
widget.lowFeedback: Not halfway yet — keep jumping toward the middle of the trip.
widget.highFeedback: Past the middle — halfway is behind you. Slide back.
widget.successFeedback: Three sixth-jumps land exactly halfway — the same spot as 1/2. Two names, one point: 3/6 = 1/2.

cml.actionGoal: Manipulate the model and track how it represents equivalent.
invariants: The manipulated model and the mathematical relationship for equivalent must stay consistent.
misconceptions: Changing a visible feature without preserving the relationship that defines equivalent.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: What change would make the model stop representing the same mathematical relationship?

explanationVariants: Equivalent fractions name one exact point — the same amount of the trip, the same amount of the bar.
2/4 and 1/2 aren't neighbors or near-misses; they are two labels glued to a single spot.

widget.prompt: 2/4 and 1/2 are equivalent. What does that mean?

options.label: They name the exact same point — the same amount
options.feedback: One spot, two names. That's the whole idea of equivalence.

options.label: They're close together on the line
options.feedback: Closer than close — they're the SAME point. Equivalence means zero gap, not a small one.

options.label: Their top numbers are equal
options.feedback: The tops differ (2 and 1)! Equivalence is about the AMOUNT the whole fraction covers, not matching digits.

options.label: 2/4 is a little more, because it has more pieces
options.feedback: More pieces, yes — but SMALLER ones. Two fourths together cover exactly what one half covers. Same amount.

steps.body: Picture two rulers on the same 0→1 trip: a halves ruler and a fourths ruler. Lay them together and the 1/2 mark sits exactly under the 2/4 mark. **Finer cuts never move points — they just hand out more names for them.**

explanationVariants: Halfway along an 8-jump trip is 4 jumps — half of 8. So 4/8 covers 1/2's point.
The eighths ruler puts a mark ON 1/2's spot and calls it 4/8 — a new name for the old point.

widget.prompt: On an EIGHTHS ruler, which mark sits on the same point as 1/2?

commonPlacements.feedback: 1/8 is one tiny jump from 0 — nowhere near halfway. Half of the 8 jumps is 4.
5/8 sits one jump PAST the middle — half of 8 jumps is exactly 4, so 4/8 is the name.
8/8 is the whole trip — that's 1, the far end. Halfway takes only half the jumps: 4/8.

widget.successFeedback: Four of eight jumps is half the trip — 1/2's spot, wearing its eighths name.
widget.lowFeedback: That mark is short of the middle — half of the 8 jumps is 4.
widget.highFeedback: That mark is past the middle — half of the 8 jumps is 4.

steps.body: Match the names that share a point.

widget.prompt: Connect each fraction to its equivalent — the name that lands on the same spot.

pairErrors.feedback: 3/6 is halfway (3 is half of 6) — that's 1/2's spot. A third of a six-jump trip is 2 jumps: 1/3 = 2/6.

widget.missFeedback: Think in sixth-jumps: halfway is 3 of 6; a third of the way is 2 of 6; the whole trip is 6 of 6.
widget.successFeedback: 1/2 = 3/6, 1/3 = 2/6, 2/2 = 6/6 — the sixths ruler renames all three points.

explanationVariants: The two fourths are each SMALLER than the one half — two smalls exactly rebuild one big. Piece counts only compare when piece sizes match.
Lay them on the bar: the two fourth-pieces tile precisely over the half. Nothing sticks out — same amount.

widget.prompt: Rio says 2/4 is MORE than 1/2 'because two pieces beat one piece.' What's the repair?

options.label: The pieces are different sizes — two fourths together cover exactly one half
options.feedback: Piece counts only settle it when piece sizes match. Here, two smalls = one big, precisely.

options.label: Rio is right — more pieces is more
options.feedback: Check it on the line: 2/4 and 1/2 stand on the SAME point. Two smaller pieces exactly rebuild the one bigger piece.

options.label: Actually 1/2 is more
options.feedback: Neither is more — that's the punchline. The two names share one spot: equivalent.

options.label: Fractions with different bottoms can never be compared
options.feedback: They can — the line compares anything. These two just happen to TIE exactly: same point.

hints: Mia's cup only shows eighth-marks — she needs 1/2's eighths name.
Half the trip means half the jumps.
explanationVariants: Half of the 8 eighth-jumps is 4 — Mia fills to the 4/8 mark, the eighths name for 1/2.
Check on the cup: 4 marks up out of 8 is exactly the middle — 1/2's spot.

widget.prompt: A recipe says 'fill the cup to 1/2.' Mia's cup only has EIGHTH marks (?/8). Which mark does she fill to? Enter the top number.

commonErrors.feedback: 2 copied the bottom of 1/2 — but on an eighths cup, the marks count EIGHTHS. Halfway up 8 marks is mark 4.
The 8/8 mark is a FULL cup — the recipe wants half. Half of the 8 marks is 4.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Half the cup = half the marks: work out half of 8.

takeaways: Equivalent = the exact same point, the exact same amount.
Finer cuts never move a point — they only add names for it.
More pieces isn't more amount when the pieces are smaller.
steps.teaser: next: WHY the amount holds still — watch a bar get traded, piece for piece.

concept.body: Quick rewind. Think of nicknames: **Sam and Samuel are one person** — two names, one kid. 1/2 and 2/4 work the same way: two names, one point on the line. Equivalent fractions never argue about who's bigger, because they're the same spot.

explanationVariants: Equivalent fractions share a single point — 2/4 stands exactly on 1/2's spot.
Two names, one place: neither is bigger, because there's only one amount being named.

options.label: The same point
options.feedback: One spot, two names — that's equivalence.

options.label: Two neighboring points
options.feedback: Zero gap between them — they stand on one shared point, not next to each other.

options.label: Two points, with 2/4 a bit farther along
options.feedback: Two fourth-jumps land exactly where one half-jump does — the same spot, no 'a bit' about it.
